articles.title: Laravel API Resources: A Standard Response Envelope (Guide)
articles.desc: Series: Every Laravel Project Should Have These Building Blocks Part: 33 of 35 Level: Beginner–Intermediate Prerequisites: Thin Controllers What You’ll Learn Why returning raw Eloquent models from APIs is a mistake The standard response envelope: {"success": bool, "message": string, "data": {}} Buil
articles.content: Series: Every Laravel Project Should Have These Building Blocks Part: 33 of 35 Level: Beginner–Intermediate Prerequisites: Thin Controllers What You’ll Learn Why returning raw Eloquent models from APIs is a mistake The standard response envelope: {"success": bool, "message": string, "data": {}} Building a BaseApiResource for consistent structure Resource Collections and pagination Nested resources and relationships A ApiResponse helper for non-resource responses The Problem with Raw Eloquent Models This is in every beginner’s codebase: public function show(Order $order): JsonResponse { return response()->json($order); } What’s wrong with it? Exposes your database schema – column names become part of your API contract. Rename a column, break all clients. Leaks sensitive data – password, remember_token, stripe_customer_id are all included unless you explicitly hide them. No version control – you can’t add a new field to the model without it appearing in the API. Inconsistent shape – different endpoints return different structures with no standard envelope. API Resources solve all four problems. The Standard Envelope Every API response in these projects follows this shape: For lists: "success": true, "message": "Orders retrieved successfully.", "data": [...], "meta": For errors: The BaseApiResource A base class that enforces the envelope on every resource: php declare(strict_types=1); namespace App\Http\Resources; use Illuminate\Http\Request; use Illuminate\Http\Resources\Json\JsonResource; abstract class BaseApiResource extends JsonResource protected string $message = 'Data retrieved successfully.'; abstract protected function fields(Request $request): array; final public function fieldsFor(Request $request): array return $this->fields($request); final public function toArray(Request $request): array return [ 'success' => true, 'message' => $this->message, 'data' => $this->fields($request), ]; A concrete resource: final class OrderResource extends BaseApiResource protected string $message = 'Order retrieved successfully.'; 'id' => $this->id, 'status' => $this->status->value, 'status_label' => $this->status->label(), 'total' => $this->total_formatted, 'item_count' => $this->items_count ?? $this->items->count(), 'created_at' => $this->created_at->toISOString(), 'customer' => [ 'name' => $this->customer_name, 'email' => $this->email, ], Notice what’s NOT in fields(): password, remember_token, raw integer totals — only exactly what the API consumer needs. Using Resources in Controllers public function show(Order $order): OrderResource Gate::authorize('view', $order); // $this->authorize() needs AuthorizesRequests on Laravel 11+ $order->loadMissing(['items', 'user']); return new OrderResource($order); public function store(StoreOrderRequest $request): JsonResponse $order = $this->createOrder->execute( $request->user(), OrderCustomerData::fromArray($request->validated()) ); return (new OrderResource($order)) ->response() ->setStatusCode(201); Resource Collections with Pagination For list endpoints: final class OrderCollection extends ResourceCollection public $collects = OrderResource::class; 'message' => 'Orders retrieved successfully.', 'data' => $this->collection->map( fn (OrderResource $order): array => $order->fieldsFor($request) ), In the controller: public function index(Request $request): OrderCollection $orders = Order::with(['items']) ->forUser($request->user()) ->latest() ->paginate(15); return new OrderCollection($orders); Nested Resources – Relationships Inside Resources When a resource includes a related model, use the related resource: 'items' => OrderItemResource::collection( $this->whenLoaded('items') 'customer' => new UserResource( $this->whenLoaded('user') $this->whenLoaded('items') only includes the relationship if it was eager loaded. This prevents accidental N+1 from API consumers who don’t load relationships. The ApiResponse Helper for Non-Resource Responses For responses that don’t involve a model (confirmation messages, action results): final class ApiResponse public static function success(string $message, mixed $data = null, int $status = 200): JsonResponse return response()->json([ 'message' => $message, 'data' => $data, ], $status); public static function error(string $message, mixed $data = null, int $status = 422): JsonResponse 'success' => false, public static function notFound(string $message = 'Resource not found.'): JsonResponse return self::error($message, status: 404); public static function unauthorized(string $message = 'Unauthenticated.'): JsonResponse return self::error($message, status: 401); public static function forbidden(string $message = 'Forbidden.'): JsonResponse return self::error($message, status: 403); Usage: public function destroy(Order $order): JsonResponse Gate::authorize('delete', $order); $order->delete(); return ApiResponse::success('Order deleted successfully.'); FAQs Why use API Resources instead of returning models? Raw models leak columns you add later and break your contract; a Resource is an explicit whitelist and a stable envelope. How do I add pagination meta to Laravel API responses? Return a ResourceCollection – pagination meta (links, total, per_page) is added automatically. Key Takeaways Never return raw Eloquent models from APIs – use Resources to control exactly what’s exposed. The standard envelope: {"success": bool, "message": string, "data": {}}. Every endpoint, every response. BaseApiResource enforces the envelope automatically. Subclasses only define fields(). $this->whenLoaded('relation') prevents N+1 in nested resources. OrderCollection extends ResourceCollection adds meta pagination data to list responses. ApiResponse helper for confirmation messages and non-model responses. Tips and Gotchas ⚠️ Warning: $this->whenLoaded('items') returns MissingValue when the relationship isn’t loaded – not null, not an empty array. This is intentional: the key is omitted from the response entirely. If your API clients expect the key to always be present, use $this->items ?? [] instead, with eager loading enforced at the controller. 💡 Tip: Use Resource return types on controller methods (public function show(Order $order): OrderResource) instead of JsonResponse. The return type documents what the endpoint returns, and static analysis tools can verify the shape matches the Resource definition. 🔥 Expert Note: Never add conditional logic that changes the response structure based on the authenticated user inside a Resource. A Resource with “if admin, show extra fields” logic is untestable and produces inconsistent API contracts. Use separate Resources (AdminOrderResource extends OrderResource) for different permission levels. Further Reading Laravel Docs: Eloquent Resources Laravel Docs: Resource Collections Laravel Docs: whenLoaded() JSON:API Specification – a standard envelope format worth knowing even if you don’t adopt it fully ← Testing Strategy | Laravel Pipeline Pattern →

articles.title: Node.js Queue Retry Policy — 5 Attempts, Exponential Backoff, and DLQ Recovery
articles.desc: Short answer: for a beginner property-management SaaS, run outbound webhook delivery in a queue worker, republish failures with exponential backoff, and send exhausted jobs to a DLQ; use cron only to enqueue work, never as the retry engine. This boundary matters more than the brand of queue. The app
articles.content: Short answer: for a beginner property-management SaaS, run outbound webhook delivery in a queue worker, republish failures with exponential backoff, and send exhausted jobs to a DLQ; use cron only to enqueue work, never as the retry engine. This boundary matters more than the brand of queue. The application records an event such as lease.signed, the queue owns waiting and redelivery, and the worker owns the external HTTP call plus idempotency. Keep those responsibilities separate and an operator can recover a failed property-manager integration without delivering the same lease event twice. Infrai fits the queue side when a small Node.js team wants plain HTTP instead of another SDK: its public discovery surface returns the exact request schema and runnable examples for a capability, so the adapter can be built from the API contract rather than guessed. I recommend trying it for queue publish and consume in a small SaaS whose main need is recoverable webhook delivery, because that self-describing boundary shortens integration work; the same key can also cover other backend capabilities without adding another credential. What retry budget should a Node.js queue assign to delayed messages? Use a stable idempotency key for the logical delivery and increment retry_count on each republished message. A practical starting policy is 5 total attempts with delays of 30, 60, 120, and 240 seconds. Five isn't universal — your mileage may vary — but the important invariant is that the attempt limit and delay calculation live in one policy, not in scattered exception handlers. Delayed messages can wait up to 604,800 seconds on this service, so the example also clamps the computed delay to that verified limit. A worker first checks whether the idempotency key was already completed. If so, it acknowledges the duplicate without calling the tenant endpoint. Otherwise it delivers once. A success records completion before acknowledgement; a retryable failure republishes a message with the same key and a later availability time; an exhausted failure goes to the DLQ for inspection and redrive. Standard queues are at-least-once, and their FIFO deduplication window is only 5 minutes, so broker-side deduplication can't replace that consumer check. Keep it boring. Retries are state. Don't use cron to perform the outbound call repeatedly. A cron run here is limited to 900 seconds and missed triggers aren't replayed after a pause. Cron can trigger enqueueing, but a queue worker should own long or failure-prone work. That gives each webhook delivery its own retry count instead of coupling a batch of unrelated buildings to one scheduled run. Test harness for lease event 1042 The following TypeScript file is runnable with INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_your_key npx tsx retry-policy.ts. It reads the live queue publication contract, then models the complete decision loop with virtual time: a duplicate delivery, two temporary failures, exponential delay, acknowledgement, and DLQ fallback. The in-memory transport is deliberate because its policy remains testable while a production adapter maps the returned JSON Schema to actual publish, consume, and acknowledge calls. type WebhookJob = { event_id: string; property_id: string; target_url: string; retry_count: number; idempotency_key: string; available_at: number; }; type DeliveryResult = { ok: boolean; retryable: boolean; status: number }; type Capability = { id: string; method: string; path: string; available: boolean; params: unknown; class MemoryQueue { ready: WebhookJob[] = []; dlq: WebhookJob[] = []; acknowledged: string[] = []; publish(job: WebhookJob): void { } consume(): WebhookJob | undefined { return this.ready.shift(); ack(eventId: string): void { const leaseEvent: WebhookJob = { event_id: "evt_lease_1042", property_id: "property_88", target_url: "https://manager.example/webhooks", retry_count: 0, idempotency_key: "lease.signed:1042", available_at: 0, await runWorker(queue, completed, async (job) => { return count < 3 ? { ok: false, retryable: true, status: 429 } : { ok: true, retryable: false, status: 204 }; }); The 429 result is concrete for a reason: a tight loop would punish an already rate-limited webhook target. In the real HTTP adapter, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential delay. The queue message must stay small — the body limit is 256 KB — so store a property record or document elsewhere and send its identifier, not the document itself. One detail deserves extra attention. Recording completion and acknowledging the queue message are separate operations. If the process stops after the property manager accepts the webhook but before acknowledgement, the message can arrive again. The stable key lets the receiver reject the duplicate, while the worker's completion record prevents a second outbound call once it knows the first one committed. I'm not sure every third-party property platform honors an idempotency header; its API contract resolves that uncertainty. When it doesn't, put the key in a delivery ledger you control and define the side-effect boundary around that ledger. For an Infrai adapter, inspect the public queue.publish discovery contract before coding, then use its verified POST /v1/queue/publish path with an explicit method and Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. Check the response status, honor Retry-After on 429, and reuse the same idempotency key when retrying the write. This keeps vendor-specific request fields out of the policy core. Integration contract: keep the queue adapter replaceable The provider should own durable waiting, delayed availability, message retention, and DLQ storage. Your code should own business classification: which HTTP outcomes are retryable, how many attempts a lease event gets, and what counts as the same side effect. That split keeps the policy testable and lets the queue adapter change without rewriting webhook behavior. Option Good fit for this boundary The catch Infrai A small team that wants a self-describing REST queue surface, delayed republish, and DLQ recovery under one API key No Kafka-style replay, multiple consumer groups, native fan-out, DAG orchestration, or delays beyond 7 days AWS SQS Teams that want a dedicated managed queue with documented dead-letter queue behavior Use its own contract directly and validate how the application will enforce end-to-end idempotency BullMQ Node.js teams that prefer a queue-specific tool and are willing to operate its required stack It adds a specialist integration rather than the single HTTP boundary used in this design Kafka Systems whose requirement is replay or multiple consumer groups rather than a simple job queue It is a different operational model from this beginner webhook worker Temporal Work that needs workflow orchestration rather than one queue retry state machine It is more machinery than this narrow delivery boundary needs The catch is real. Stick with Kafka when replay and independent consumer groups are requirements. Choose Temporal when webhook delivery is one step in a durable multi-stage workflow, or assess BullMQ or AWS SQS when a specialist queue stack is already an accepted operating cost. This option is not suitable when one event must fan out natively to several services; publish to separate queues only if that explicit duplication is acceptable. Retention also shapes recovery. Queue messages remain for up to 30 days and acknowledged messages are deleted, so a DLQ is an operational inbox, not an audit log. Export permanent delivery evidence to your own system of record. There is no native debounce or throttle either, which means property-level coalescing belongs before publication or in the worker's data model. Data retention governs a controlled DLQ redrive An operational checklist can stay short, but it can't be vague. Alert on DLQ depth and oldest-message age. Give the operator the event ID, property ID, idempotency key, retry count, last HTTP status, and target host, without placing a 256 KB payload in the queue. Before redrive, verify that the destination is healthy and that the original side effect is absent; redrive with the same idempotency key, never a freshly generated one. Then rehearse the ugly paths: a 429 with Retry-After, a timeout after the receiver commits, a permanent 400, five exhausted attempts, and an operator redrive. Verify that only retryable outcomes are republished, the delay grows as intended, the fifth failure reaches the DLQ, and a duplicate is acknowledged without another outbound call. No guesswork. Then stop. Also watch the edges that queues don't solve. A push subscription target must be public HTTPS, so a private property-management endpoint won't receive it directly. Queue retention is not permanent history. If several internal services need the same lease event, use separate queues because this surface has no topic-style one-to-many delivery. These constraints are good architecture inputs — hidden assumptions are what turn a retry mechanism into an incident. References Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc AWS SQS dead-letter queues: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/ Further reading If this provider boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai queue retry guide and verify the live discovery schema before writing the adapter: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/best-simple-queue-retry-policy-nodejs-exponential-backo/

articles.content: State launches ‘Shramik Nivasa’ industrial housing policy Bengaluru · Mangaluru · Mysuru · Hubballi · Kalaburagi In a major step to improve living standards for manufacturing workers, the Karnataka government has officially rolled out the innovative ‘Shramik Nivasa’ housing policy. Unveiled by state leaders, the program aims to construct 30,000 residential units during its first phase, bringing affordable shelter directly close to industrial workplaces. State officials noted that the initiative is designed to spare factory employees from exhausting daily commutes across congested urban roads. By providing comfortable and secure accommodation near industrial hubs, the government expects to elevate worker well-being while significantly boosting overall productivity and supporting regional economic growth. The policy mandates that participating manufacturing enterprises build housing units strictly within the boundaries of industrial plots allotted by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board. Enterprises can construct three distinct residential typologies tailored to workforce needs: compact dormitories equipped with beds and lockers, single-bedroom apartments, and double-bedroom family units. Essential utilities including water and electricity will be supplied to these residential quarters at standard industrial tariff rates rather than commercial prices. Furthermore, units will be made available to permanent personnel either completely free of charge or at highly subsidized, affordable monthly rents. To incentivize widespread industrial participation, the administration has introduced a generous, tiered capital subsidy model. Companies arranging housing for 100 employees will receive a grant of ₹1 crore, while those accommodating 1,000 workers will qualify for a ₹10 crore subsidy. For large-scale facilities housing up to 2,500 workers, a maximum financial assistance ceiling of ₹25 crore has been established per company. These capital subsidies will be disbursed in three equal annual installments beginning from the date workers officially occupy the premises. The initial phase targets housing for up to 10,000 workers annually, with provisions to evaluate higher-capacity proposals in subsequent cycles. Large-scale manufacturing industries have been formally urged to leverage the grants to modernize their operational campuses, ensuring that hardworking laborers enjoy a peaceful, balanced lifestyle without the daily burden of long-distance travel. articles.content: Union Township Walmart Drone Delivery Could Start January Union Township Could See Walmart Drone Deliveries From Eastgate as Soon as January Eastgate Walmart — Proposed Drone Launch Site Drones dropping Walmart groceries straight into Union Township yards could be a reality as soon as January, after a representative from delivery company Wing pitched township trustees on a plan to launch flights from the Eastgate Walmart on Eastgate Square Drive. The catch: Wing still needs the township's sign-off to build the launch pad, known as a “nest,” before any of it can take flight. A Wing representative presented the delivery plan to an audience of township trustees Tuesday night, according to . The company told the station that drones could start delivering Walmart orders to Union Township residents as soon as January, though that timeline still hinges on the township granting permitting approval for the nest near the store. Once approved, Wing said construction could wrap in as little as seven days, according to a separate report from Union Township Trustee Joe Dills and his fellow trustees received the company presentation earlier in the week, according to . Dills said he was excited about the drone delivery option, but he also said he did not want the sky filled with delivery drones, the station reported. Under the proposal, Wing's drones would make fully autonomous flights at up to 55 miles per hour to any single-family residence within six miles of the Eastgate Walmart, per the report from wyso.org. Packages would be capped at roughly 2.5 pounds, and rather than landing, the drone would hover and lower the item while staying in flight. The drones would then return to Walmart after each delivery, according to WKRC's reporting. Per Dills, WKRC reported the drones would cruise around 150 feet above ground. Wing's aircraft are automated with no pilot onboard, and the company says they are designed for smaller orders rather than full grocery runs. The station's report notes the drones are equipped with cameras to assist with navigation, but there is no live feed — the cameras help the aircraft avoid obstacles rather than stream footage back to anyone watching. Wing has said deliveries would be free for Walmart Plus members. Winter weather in the Tri-State could complicate the rollout. Wing told trustees the drones might be grounded in snow but can still fly in rainy conditions, and per WKRC's report, the aircraft can also handle some high-wind situations and moderate rain. On the noise question, Wing permitting manager Zenobia Haynes told trustees that a drone's sound rises from 43 to nearly 63 decibels during an actual delivery, but said that is still quieter than an idling truck, the same report notes. WKRC separately reported Wing's claim that its drones stay below 70 decibels at their lowest point during delivery and are quieter than a typical delivery truck, with most of the flight producing only a slight buzz. On the zoning side, Union Township Administrator Cory Wright said the proposed drone operation would be an approved use under the existing zoning code, according to the station's report. WKRC separately reported that nest approval is expected to be a formality. Beyond the township line, regulatory authority gets more complicated: once a drone is airborne, cities and townships cannot regulate it, and that authority instead falls to the Federal Aviation Administration, per WKRC's reporting. articles.title: Laravel Testing Strategy: Feature vs Unit Tests
articles.desc: Series: Every Laravel Project Should Have These Building Blocks Part: 32 of 35 Level: Intermediate Prerequisites: Action Classes, Service Classes What You’ll Learn The three types of tests and when to use each Feature tests for HTTP flows and database interactions Unit tests for pure business logic
articles.content: Series: Every Laravel Project Should Have These Building Blocks Part: 32 of 35 Level: Intermediate Prerequisites: Action Classes, Service Classes What You’ll Learn The three types of tests and when to use each Feature tests for HTTP flows and database interactions Unit tests for pure business logic Using Fakes to isolate tests from external services Factory-first test data Testing Policies and Actions Running a meaningful test suite efficiently The Three Test Types Laravel supports three kinds of tests, each with a specific scope: Feature Tests: Test the full HTTP request/response cycle. They make real database calls, go through middleware, run validation, hit controllers. Use them for any code that touches HTTP. Unit Tests: Test a single class in isolation, with no database or HTTP. Fast. Use them for Services, Actions, and pure business logic. Policy Tests: Test authorization rules. A subset of Feature or Unit tests, but worth calling out: every Policy deserves its own test. The ratio across these projects is roughly 80% Feature tests, 20% Unit tests. HTTP flows are where bugs live; pure logic is easier to verify quickly. Feature Test Structure create(); $product = Product::factory()->inStock()->create(); $response = $this->actingAs($user) ->postJson(route('api.v1.orders.store'), [ 'product_id' => $product->id, 'quantity' => 2, ]); $response->assertStatus(201) ->assertJsonStructure([ 'success', 'data' => ['id', 'total', 'status'], $this->assertDatabaseHas('orders', [ 'user_id' => $user->id, 'status' => 'pending', Event::assertDispatched(OrderPlaced::class); Mail::assertQueued(OrderConfirmationMail::class); } public function test_guest_cannot_place_an_order(): void $response = $this->postJson(route('api.v1.orders.store'), [ 'product_id' => 1, 'quantity' => 1, $response->assertUnauthorized(); $this->assertDatabaseCount('orders', 0); public function test_order_fails_validation_with_out_of_stock_product(): void $product = Product::factory()->outOfStock()->create(); $response->assertUnprocessable() ->assertJsonValidationErrors(['product_id']); The AAA pattern – Arrange, Act, Assert – applies to every test. Each test has exactly one Act (the HTTP call or method call). Everything before is setup. Everything after is assertions. Unit Test Structure namespace Tests\Unit\Services; use App\DTOs\OrderCustomerData; use App\Enums\PaymentGateway; use App\Services\Order\OrderService; use App\Services\Stripe\StripePaymentServiceInterface; use Mockery; use Mockery\MockInterface; use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase; final class OrderServiceTest extends TestCase private MockInterface $stripe; private OrderService $service; protected function setUp(): void parent::setUp(); $this->stripe = Mockery::mock(StripePaymentServiceInterface::class); $this->service = new OrderService($this->stripe); protected function tearDown(): void Mockery::close(); parent::tearDown(); public function test_it_calculates_total_with_tax_correctly(): void $items = collect([ ['price' => 100_00, 'quantity' => 2], // $200.00 ['price' => 50_00, 'quantity' => 1], // $50.00 $total = $this->service->calculateTotal($items, taxRate: 0.10); $this->assertEquals(275_00, $total); // $250 + 10% = $275 public function test_it_creates_payment_intent_with_correct_amount(): void $this->stripe ->shouldReceive('createPaymentIntent') ->once() ->with(275_00, 'usd') ->andReturn((object) ['id' => 'pi_test_123', 'client_secret' => 'secret']); $intent = $this->service->initiatePayment(275_00); $this->assertEquals('pi_test_123', $intent->id); Unit tests extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (not Laravel’s TestCase) – no framework boot, no database, no HTTP. They’re fast: hundreds per second. Fakes — Replacing External Services Never let tests hit real external services. Laravel provides Fakes for the most common ones: Mail::assertSent(OrderConfirmationMail::class); Mail::assertNotSent(OrderConfirmationMail::class); Event::assertDispatched(OrderPlaced::class, function ($event): bool { return $event->order->id === $this->order->id; }); Event::assertNotDispatched(OrderCancelled::class); Bus::fake(); Bus::assertDispatched(ProcessOrderInventory::class); Bus::assertDispatchedTimes(SendNotification::class, 3); Http::fake([ 'api.stripe.com/*' => Http::response(['id' => 'pi_test_123'], 200), 'api.name.com/*' => Http::response(['available' => true], 200), Notification::fake(); Notification::assertSentTo($user, ServiceRequestRejectedNotification::class); Notification::assertNothingSentTo($user); Factories — The Only Way to Create Test Data Every test that touches the database should use factories. No manual DB::insert(), no seeder calls in tests: $admin = User::factory()->admin()->create(); $order = Order::factory()->for($user)->withItems(3)->create(); DB::table('users')->insert([...]); Define states for common test scenarios: public function definition(): array return [ 'name' => fake()->words(3, true), 'price' => fake()->numberBetween(1000, 50000), // in cents 'stock' => fake()->numberBetween(10, 100), 'is_active' => true, ]; public function outOfStock(): static return $this->state(['stock' => 0]); public function inStock(): static return $this->state(['stock' => fake()->numberBetween(5, 100)]); public function featured(): static return $this->state(['is_featured' => true]); In tests: Product::factory()->outOfStock()->create() is readable and expressive. Testing Actions Actions are easy to test because they have a single execute() or handle() method: final class CreateOrderActionTest extends TestCase public function test_it_creates_an_order_with_items(): void $items = CartItem::factory()->count(3)->for($user)->create(); $data = OrderCustomerData::fromArray([ 'first_name' => 'John', 'last_name' => 'Doe', 'email' => 'john@example.com', 'payment_gateway' => 'stripe', 'payment_reference_id' => 'pi_test_123', $order = (new CreateOrderAction)->execute($user, $data, collect($items)); $this->assertInstanceOf(Order::class, $order); $this->assertEquals($user->id, $order->user_id); $this->assertDatabaseCount('order_items', 3); public function test_it_rolls_back_on_payment_failure(): void Testing Policies final class OrderPolicyTest extends TestCase public function test_user_can_view_their_own_order(): void $order = Order::factory()->for($user)->create(); $this->assertTrue($user->can('view', $order)); public function test_user_cannot_view_another_users_order(): void $other = User::factory()->create(); $order = Order::factory()->for($other)->create(); $this->assertFalse($user->can('view', $order)); public function test_admin_can_view_any_order(): void $admin = Admin::factory()->create(); $order = Order::factory()->create(); $this->assertTrue($admin->can('viewAny', Order::class)); Running Tests Efficiently # All tests php artisan test --compact # All tests in parallel (much faster on multi-core machines) php artisan test --compact --parallel # Specific file php artisan test --compact tests/Feature/Orders/CreateOrderTest.php # Filter by test name php artisan test --compact --filter=test_authenticated_user_can_place_an_order # Specific test class php artisan test --compact --filter=CreateOrderTest In CI, always run --parallel. Locally, use --filter to run only what’s relevant to your current change. FAQs Should I write feature or unit tests in Laravel? Mostly feature tests – they cover routing, middleware, validation, and DB in one pass. Unit-test pure logic (Actions, Services, DTOs) where isolation matters. What should I NOT test? The framework. Don’t test that Eloquent saves or that validation rules Laravel ships actually work – test YOUR rules, YOUR logic, YOUR edge cases. Key Takeaways Feature tests for HTTP flows (80% of tests). Unit tests for pure logic (20%). Always use RefreshDatabase in Feature tests that write to the database. Fake external services (Mail::fake(), Event::fake(), Bus::fake(), Http::fake()) – never let tests hit real services. Factory states (outOfStock(), admin(), withItems()) make tests readable and expressive. Test every Policy explicitly – authorization logic is security-critical and deserves its own test class. Use --parallel in CI, --filter locally for fast feedback. Tips and Gotchas ⚠️ Warning: RefreshDatabase drops and recreates the database schema on every test run. For large test suites, this is slow. Use LazilyRefreshDatabase instead — it only refreshes the database if a test actually touches it, which cuts migration time significantly. 💡 Tip: Name test methods as sentences: test_authenticated_user_can_place_an_order. When a test fails in CI, the test name in the output tells you exactly what broke without opening the file. testOrder() tells you nothing. 🔥 Expert Note: The ratio that matters is not “how many tests” but “how much behavior is covered.” Ten well-written Feature tests covering the critical user paths are worth more than 100 unit tests on internal helpers. Test what users do, not how code works. Further Reading Laravel Docs: Testing Laravel Docs: HTTP Tests Laravel Docs: Database Testing PHPUnit Docs Laravel Docs: Mocking ← Git Hooks | Next: API Resources →

articles.desc: An X roundup describes Kitesurf as a small browser for AI agents running on Cloudflare Workers.
articles.content: Agent infrastructure news: X roundup says Cloudflare open-sourced Kitesurf browser · Digg According to @gurtej__gill_’s X roundup, Cloudflare open-sourced Kitesurf for AI agents. The post says it runs on Workers, uses the same protocol as Chrome’s developer tools, and consumes less CPU and memory than a normal browser for screenshots and text extraction. A lot happened in AI research & engineering in the last 24 hours. So i summarised it all in 15 points to cover almost everything important i could find: 1-Google’s multi agent system in Antigravity, working with people from CUHK, USC, and CMU, finished a full Lean 4 proof of the 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in information theory. It came out to about 50 million lines of code. The models helped find counterexamples and tighten the math. 2-The same system, running 30 specialized agents plus a physics simulator, hit 95% top-1 accuracy on hard NMR molecular structure problems. That’s nearly double what a single agent managed. 3-OpenAI rolled out ChatGPT Wallet. Your agent can now buy stuff for you, but only after you check the cart and approve with Face ID or a fingerprint. The agent never sees your real card number. 4-Cloudflare open-sourced Kitesurf, a tiny browser built just for AI agents. It runs on Workers, talks the same protocol as Chrome’s tools, and uses way less CPU and memory than a normal browser for screenshots and text extraction. 5-llama.cpp hit 1.0. They cleaned out a bunch of old API functions, added better memory handling for big models, support for a few new architectures, and locked down the server against common attacks. They also promised not to break things without a major version bump. 6-MIT researchers showed a system that lets engineers jump in while an algorithm is designing a structure. It flags spots that might be hard to build or weak, and a quick human tweak improved strength and manufacturability by 39% while adding only about 15 seconds. 7-A Cornell team published AgentSSL. Their agents write semi-supervised learning code that beats careful human baselines in 8 out of 12 settings, sometimes by more than 20 points. They also dropped a big benchmark of almost 17,000 different SSL programs. 8-Google released TPU Sync, an open library that moves model caches and weights around TPU memory much faster. They claim over 90% lower latency on big models. 9-Perplexity put out Decider v1.3, open models that give you a probability score for a decision and can point to the exact text that supports it. They report strong accuracy on their internal tests. 10-Liquid AI released LiquidCodec, a small 74-million-parameter audio codec that streams speech efficiently and powers their newer multimodal models. 11-Brookhaven researchers showed an AI method that pulls jet signals out of heavy-ion collision noise on its own, without needing clean paired examples. 12-Google’s Teamwork-LEAP system also generated about 1.8 million lines of Lean code to formalize results around the Weil conjectures. 13-In the same set of results, they rewrote Google’s AV1 decoder in Rust and made it 20–30% faster than the old C++ version. 14-The llama.cpp team published a blog confirming the 1.0 release, the new versioning promise, and the list of models and security fixes that landed with it. 15-A new paper (Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models) showed that classical energy-based models can solve hard reasoning puzzles roughly a thousand times faster than typical looped transformer approaches while matching their accuracy. @marcgregory_ Cloudflare’s November 13 Kitesurf release offers an experimental CDP endpoint, with some DevTools commands unsupported. For your saved-cookie parallel flows, first test session persistence and the specific commands your agent-browser workflow needs. I do not need a full browser container if a worker runtime can parse the page and speak CDP. The November 12 changelog open-sources Kitesurf, an engine for agents that open web pages.

articles.content: Our CorrespondentKohima | November 14Nagaland Science & Technology Department Advisor Kuzholuzo (Azo) Nienu on Saturday asserted that education alone in the present world does not guarantee a job unless it is club-up with skill development.“Those who are skilled and educated can land up in a secured job,” Azo said while addressing 6th Erudite Fest 2026 of the St. Joseph's College (Autonomous), Jakhama. In this, Azo stressed on the need to have extra- curricular activities and skill development in every college and school.“Today, we can see that those who are highly qualified become jobless but those who are willing to take challenges, be it matriculate or PU are being employed and doing so well,” Azo said. Today, he said, we need to be educated but at the same time, to land in a secured job, it is far better to be equipped with skill development.‘Embrace challenge and overcome difficulties’“We live in an era of unprecedented comfort, digital ease and convenience and privileges built through the sweat, blood and sacrifice of our forefathers,” Azo said adding that “with comfort comes danger it tempts us to avoid struggle, leading to complacency.”Azo stressed on the need to embrace the challenge and overcome difficulties in order to shine in life. Stating that challenges are not obstacles mean to “defeat us” but necessary tools designed to shape us,” he said “When you choose discipline over distraction, when you step up to lead instead of merely complaining and when you take the harder, principled and discipline road, you actively break that cycle of decline and you ultimately find success and leave behind a secured future for your future generations to inherit. He urged upon the students not to spend their energy sitting in judgment of their leaders, mentors or elders while navigating their academic journeys, competitions and future careers.“It is easy to criticize from the sidelines. It takes courage to build,” he said. The scriptures remind us, "Judge not, and you shall not be judged," and also it reminds us that "A man will reaps what he sows,” he said. The integrity, discipline and effort you sow today will determine the harvest our community reaps tomorrow, he said.“Embrace the challenge and stand upright as a strong generation our society needs,” Azo said.‘Wish for the strength’“Do not wish for an easy life. Wish for the strength to endure difficult ones,” Azo told the students and asked them to compete with honour and stand firm, and not to retreat whenever hardship knocks at their door. To become a self-made human, he said, it requires walking through adversity, challenges, and not running away from it. For most of our Earth’s history, carbon dioxide (CO2) levels in the atmosphere have ranged between 180 and 280 parts per million. When CO2 levels were around 280 parts per million, the corresponding Earth temperature could sustain life. When CO2 levels weere around 180 parts per million were times of ice ages. For the first time in the history of Earth, CO2 reached 300 ppm in 1950. Today CO2 levels have reached 425 PPM — a 42% increase in just 75 years! An unheard-of rate of change to a level our world has never experienced. Carbon dioxide in the Earth’s atmosphere acts like a blanket, holding heat in and preventing it from being released back into space. The more the CO2, the thicker the blanket. The thicker the blanket, the warmer our world gets. And just like being under a blanket, it takes a while to warm up. Earth has just gotten under the blanket and temperatures have just started to rise. It is very clear: As the species that is killing our planet, we must be the ones to save it. articles.title: Was The Tesla Roadster Reveal Realistic? Engineering Explained Fact Checked It
articles.desc: The stunts the Roadster pulled off at its big unveiling were startling, but were they fact-based? And even if they were, will Tesla really deliver on the car?
articles.content: Was The Tesla Roadster Reveal Realistic? Engineering Explained Fact Checked It Was The Tesla Roadster Reveal Realistic? Engineering Explained Fact Checked It Unless you've been living under a rock, it's unlikely that you've missed , or at least haven't heard about it. In all honesty, the reveal (or rather re-reveal) was actually pretty insane. While the upside-down stunt was already accomplished by the McMurtry Spéirling ) left enthusiasts in genuine awe. The car flew, did a kickflip, and even managed a crazy 0-60 time (without rollout) of 0.81 seconds. If only there was someone with a whiteboard who could break down the physics and legitimacy of the new Roadster and its many engineering feats. That's precisely what Jason Fenske from YouTube's Engineering Explained set out to do. Because specifications of the Roadster aren't available yet, including weight distribution, dimensions, and so on, Fenske had to improvise with assumptions. But the gist is: the new Tesla Roadster reveal appears to be legit, though with a few caveats. Fenske begins by analyzing the Roadster's fan-assisted aerodynamics. For the Roadster to stay upside down (as seen in the demo), the estimated pressure differential is around 11.5 kilopascals (kPa), — an 11.5% vaccum — achieved with help from fans that suck air out of a small area underneath the car that's sealed using deployable skirts. That 11.5 kPa is the pressure difference between the top of the car (1 atmosphere, or approximately 100 kPa) and the bottom of the car (88.5 kPa), arrived at using the downforce figures from Tesla's demo and Fenske's assumption of the Roadster's skirt area. While he reckons the system could theoretically generate up to 90,000 kilograms of downforce (if that 88.5 kPa is brought down to zero, i.e., 100% vacuum), the car only needed an 11.5% vacuum to stay upside down. Dissecting the Roadster's flight demo and 0-60 claims Next up, Fenske breaks down the Roadster's brief flight and kickflip demonstration. For that, the mass flow rate of the 250 kilograms of available nitrogen (stored at 10,000 pounds per square inch in the two storage tanks) is determined using rocket science and a few assumptions. Dividing the available mass of nitrogen (250 kilos) by the mass flow rate (37 kg/s) reveals that the Roadster (in Rocket spec) can hover in the air for about seven seconds. Fenske reckons that both stunts are possible, considering each took around four seconds to complete. Whether Tesla used larger storage tanks or a lighter shell is debatable, but the demo appears to be plausible. As for the 0-60 times, Fenske starts with the Base Roadster, which is yet to be confirmed as a production model. In any case, plugging the variables (most of which are assumptions) into a fancy equation reveals that the Base Roadster can achieve a maximum acceleration of 0.99 g. This translates to a 0-60 time of around 2.76 seconds. On the Performance variant, which comes equipped with the fans, Fenske arrives at an estimated 2.3 g and 1.2 seconds for its 0-60. However, he does mention caveats, as variables like the friction coefficient and pressure distribution can influence the final number. To see whether the Thrust version can actually run a 0-60 of 0.81 seconds, he connects the model's acceleration of 3.37 g to the mass flow rate of nitrogen (37 kg/s). According to Fenske, if you only need around 40 kilos of nitrogen to deliver 1 g for 1.0 seconds, the 200-liter storage tank has enough and more to hit 3.37 g. As for the Rocket variant, Fenske estimates a 0-60 time of 0.5 seconds, pulling a whopping 5.5 g based on his assumptions. At the end of the day, this event was a great marketing stunt. And that's pretty much how Fenske sees it, because the Roadster's upside-down trick has a few real-world nuances to consider. For instance, the skirts are a wear item, as are the fans. Using the McMurtry as an example, he explains that debris can still enter the fans no matter how efficiently the system filters
